title: Payment System & Double-Entry Ledger
intro: Architect a mission-critical payment processing system guaranteeing exactly-once charge semantics, idempotency, and audit-compliant double-entry accounting.
objectives: Enforce strict API idempotency using unique Idempotency Keys and distributed mutexes.
Implement double-entry bookkeeping: $\sum \text{Debits} = \sum \text{Credits}$ at all times.
Design asynchronous payment gateway reconciliation and settlement batch workers.
body:
### The Idempotency Protocol
Network calls fail unpredictably. When a client times out waiting for a payment response, it retries. Without idempotency, the customer is billed twice.
1. Client generates UUID `Idempotency-Key` header with charge request.
2. Server attempts atomic insert of key in Redis/DB with status `PROCESSING`.
3. If duplicate key arrives while processing, server returns `HTTP 409 Conflict` or waits.
4. Once payment gateway (Stripe) succeeds, server saves final response payload mapped to the key. Subsequent retries immediately return cached `HTTP 200 OK`.

### Double-Entry Accounting Invariant
Money cannot be created or destroyed. Every transaction consists of matched Debit and Credit entries:
$$\sum \text{Debits} - \sum \text{Credits} = 0$$
Never store user balances as mutable raw numbers; compute balance from immutable ledger audit rows.
keyIdea: Money systems must be strictly idempotent and backed by immutable double-entry ledgers. Always reconcile external payment gateway logs asynchronously.

concepts.title: Reconciliation Engine
concepts.body: Daily batch worker comparing internal ledger records with external payment processor bank settlement files (BAI2 / MT940).

examples: Stripe API idempotency design handling billions of transactions.

quiz.prompt: What core rule governs double-entry bookkeeping in payment ledgers?
options: Every transaction must contain equal matching debit and credit entries with net sum zero
User balances must be stored in volatile RAM caches
Transactions can only be executed during banking hours
quiz.explanation: Double-entry accounting requires every balance transfer to record equal debits and credits, preserving total system balance.
